doc.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013

title: Avant-garde musicians and publicity; the Cavett show
summary: Archie Shepp's provocations, the avant-garde's publicity-consciousness, Ornette, and the Jazz and People's Movement on the Cavett show.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: I see. Do you think those musicians who were playing, I mean Archie Schepp’s music, just to use his name with that genre, this is music that’s let’s say challenging for the average listener. Do you think that they honestly thought that if they got the right amount of exposure in magazines and the media that they could sell more records?

Yes, absolutely. I mean Archie, who is a very clever fellow and very sophisticated, was perfectly aware that doing things, writing, expressing himself verbally and doing things that were to some extent deliberately provocative, that that should result in people wanting to check out his music and also that he might enlist people who were politically on the same wavelength and so on. Yes, absolutely. And it must be said that the avante

garde in jazz was very publicity-conscious. They were very much aware of the fact that if they were making provocative statements and all these things — and the music itself of course was aggressive, some of it. Interestingly enough, I mean Ornette’s music was never — Ornette very rarely, although he sometimes said things — he usually had to do with recognition of his music rather than putting it on a more universal social-political platform. It was always very personal with Ornette. And Ornette’s music was a thing unto itself. But it was a very interesting period. And there was the attempt with the “Jazz and People’s Movement” to get exposure on television, which was perfectly reasonable. You know jazz was never sufficiently well exposed on T.V. But the way they went about it, and what they eventually managed to accomplish, was counterproductive. I mean that was — I was closely involved in that because we had controversies in the pages of DownBeat. But they went on the Cavett show. They picketed these various television shows. Merv Griffin, Cavett, and Ed Sullivan. And on Cavett, because Cavett was always — you know he was a very verbal guy, so he put musicians on a panel and talked to them and there was Andy Cyrille and Freddie Hubbard and Cecil Taylor. And my God, you know that discussion was totally — it would not have appealed to anyone who didn’t have some really inside knowledge of the music and it was off-putting, because it was simply — it addressed issues that the average listener had nothing to do with. And then they also said stupid things. Like Freddie, whom I was very fond of and who, poor guy, I mean what he went through and he messed up his embouchure and it was embarrassing to see him trying to play and then the poor guy died you know. But that was a long time ago. He was young and brash and everything. Well he said, notably, one totally off the wall thing, he said that Coleman Hawkins was wrapping packages in Queens. Coleman Hawkins first of all never went near Queens, and secondly he had — although his health was declining he had a beautiful apartment in Central Park West, he had a Chrysler Imperial parked — it was rusting because he wasn’t using it, but God knows — so this was really dumb stuff. And then they got on Sullivan and gave them a closing five minutes. Do you remember that?
